sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Odessa, Texas?
sections.html:
Odessa homeowners pay several taxing units on one account, and the Ector County Appraisal District is the first office to call. The Texas Comptroller's county directory lists the City of Odessa, Ector County, Ector County ISD, the Odessa Junior College District, a county hospital district, a utility district and two emergency service districts among the active taxing units.

The same directory says the Ector County tax assessor-collector's office does not collect property tax, and that in a county like that the appraisal district may be the collector. The appraisal district's own site describes its job as appraisal and tax collection, and it publishes 432-332-6834 for questions about amounts due. Its office is at 1301 E. 8th St. in Odessa.

Some Odessa addresses fall in Midland County. The city's budget FAQ states that the city does not set values, and that the Ector County or Midland County appraisal district does, depending on where the property sits. Confirm which district holds your parcel before you look up an account or file a protest.

sections.h2: What is the Odessa city property tax rate?
sections.html:
The city's 2026-27 taxpayer impact statement lists $0.471578 per $100 of valuation for the city's share of the bill. The prior year's rate on the same page is $0.470700. The city's FAQ says it spends property tax on firefighters, police officers, road repairs and parks.

The city rate is only one slice of what you owe. The school district, county, college, hospital district and any special district add their own rates to the same account.

Odessa's FAQ compares the city with its neighbors. It lists Midland's proposed 2026-27 rate at $0.383092, Lubbock's at $0.482106 and Abilene's at $0.7496. It also reports average home appraisals of $201,754 in Odessa and $402,171 in Midland, which is why Midland collects more gross tax revenue ($62.1 million against about $46.0 million for Odessa) at a lower rate.

Property tax supplies 15.8 percent of the city's revenue, and sales tax supplies 18.2 percent. The city's piece of sales tax is 1.25 percent of the 8.25 percent total.

sections.h2: When is Odessa property tax due, and what does a late payment cost?
sections.html:
Bills go out around October 1 and the tax is due by January 31, so an unpaid balance is delinquent on February 1. When the unit mails a bill after January 10, the delinquency date can move to the first of a later month that allows at least 21 days.

  • February 1: a six percent penalty and one percent interest are added.
  • Each month after: the penalty grows one percent a month until July 1, when it reaches 12 percent. Interest keeps running at one percent a month with no ceiling.
  • Units with a collection contract can add an attorney penalty of up to 20 percent.
  • Split option: pay half by November 30 and the rest by June 30 of the next year.

Owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, may pay in four installments on a residence homestead. A homestead owner who is already delinquent can ask a collector for a payment plan of up to 36 months, though only a homestead has a right to one. To ask for a waiver of penalty and interest, pay within 21 days of learning about the delinquency and request the waiver in writing before the 181st day.

sections.h2: How can an Odessa homeowner lower the tax bill?
sections.html:
Start with the homestead exemption, then check the appraisal notice every spring. The appraisal district posts a 2026 sheet called Exemption Amounts by Entity that lists what each Odessa-area taxing unit gives, including the city, the county and the college.

  • School homestead exemption: $140,000 off the value for school district tax.
  • Age 65 or older, or disabled: an extra $60,000 for school tax. A person who gets the over-65 exemption loses the separate disabled one.
  • Local option: a unit may exempt up to 20 percent of value, with a floor of $5,000.
  • Appraisal cap: a homestead's appraised value cannot rise more than 10 percent a year, counted from the year after the exemption begins.
  • School tax ceiling: for owners 65 or older or disabled, the school tax on the homestead is generally frozen at the first qualifying year's level.

File the exemption application with the appraisal district before May 1. A new buyer who closes after January 1 may claim the exemption for the rest of that year if the seller did not have it. Disabled veterans use a separate exemption that scales with the VA rating, up to $12,000 in the 70 to 100 percent band, and a veteran rated 100 percent gets a full exemption on the residence homestead.

To protest a value, file by May 15 or within 30 days after the notice was delivered, whichever is later. After the appraisal review board rules, an owner may go to district court, binding arbitration, or the State Office of Administrative Hearings when the board's value is over $1,000,000.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Odessa property tax when the house is sold?
sections.html:
The tax follows the property. A lien attaches on January 1 for that year's tax, and a buyer cannot get clear title until the delinquent amounts are paid. The owner on January 1 stays liable for that year's bill even after a sale, so a closing statement should show how the year's tax is split.

If delinquent tax goes to a sale, the former owner of a homestead has two years from the date the buyer's deed is filed to redeem, and other property has 180 days. Redemption costs include a premium over the bid. Any money left after a tax foreclosure can be claimed by the former owner for two years after the sale.

Odessa adds a few city rules a seller meets before listing. Residential building permits come from the city's Building Inspection division at 411 W. 8th Street, by phone at 432-335-3214 or through the online portal. A sidewalk, driveway or curb the city engineer finds defective becomes the adjoining owner's duty to repair within 30 days of notice, and a landlord must keep working smoke detectors in rental units.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show about Odessa housing?
sections.html:
Odessa covers 51.08 square miles of land and counted 114,428 people in the 2020 Census, with a July 2025 estimate of 122,707. About 59.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the 2020-2024 median value of an owned home is $223,100.

Median household income is $73,472, and median gross rent is $1,315 a month. The average worker spends 22.4 minutes getting to work. These are citywide figures, so a specific street can differ a lot, and a house's own appraisal is what drives its bill.

faqs.q: Is Odessa property tax due on January 31?
faqs.a: Yes. Tax for the year is due by January 31 and is delinquent from February 1. Penalty and interest start that day, with a six percent penalty and one percent interest, and the penalty reaches 12 percent on July 1.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property tax to in Odessa?
faqs.a: Start with the Ector County Appraisal District at 432-332-6834. The Comptroller's directory says the Ector County tax assessor-collector does not collect property tax and that the appraisal district may collect it. If your property lies in Midland County, ask that county's appraisal district instead.

faqs.q: What is the Odessa city tax rate for 2026-27?
faqs.a: The city's taxpayer impact statement shows $0.471578 per $100 of valuation. That is the city's portion only, and the school district, county, college and other units bill separately on top of it.

faqs.q: Does Odessa have its own homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Ask the appraisal district for its 2026 Exemption Amounts by Entity sheet, which lists what the City of Odessa and each other unit grants. The school district exemption of $140,000 is set by state law, and any other unit may add an optional exemption of up to 20 percent of value, not less than $5,000.

faqs.q: What if I sell an Odessa house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: The lien on the property comes with it, so the taxes are normally paid at closing from the proceeds. A buyer cannot get clear title until the delinquent tax is cleared, and the owner on January 1 stays personally liable for that year's bill.
